quotedTweet.text:
on writing - something I wish I'd learned MUCH earlier

"always write the first page last"

prob wasted hundreds, if not thousands, of hours by not sticking to this...it matters more and more as you write longer pieces.

(1/5)

what happens when you start with the intro - "here's what this paper/article/pitch is going to be about" - is that you run into multiple problems

first...as you're writing, you'll usually find that you're starting to deviate from the intro/first page.

this is natural and probably a sign that what you're writing is good (organic, from the heart, not mechanical)

so then you go back to the first page and re-write it..."now THIS is what its about."

(2/5)

this process repeats itself and once you get into real long-form, 20, 50, 100+ pages, the first page becomes a form of torture

you can easily waste an entire day writing and re-writing a one-page introduction. plus you enter a circular feedback loop and begin questioning, like, did I write what I meant to write? are these 100 pages all dogshit? what the fuck am I doing?

writing is impossibly hard because you CAN move backwards. there is no guarantee that incremental time + effort creates better results...you can over-edit something good into something bad.

Orwell: "Writing a book is a horrible, exhausting struggle, like a long bout of some painful illness. One would never undertake such a thing if one were not driven on by some demon whom one can neither resist or understand."

(3/5)

this applies for stocks as well

if you sit down and open with "heres why abcd is a long," and then go thru the entire rsch process with this preconceived bias, you'll start running into major issues as you inevitably dig up disconfirming facts

I look back at bosses I had, some would say "go look at abcd as a long," but the real good ones would just say "go take a look at abcd." 

I could usually guess what their inclination was but the write-up always came out better because it was borne from a place of objectivity and "lets see where the facts take me."

this is Pascal's "I would've written a shorter letter, but I didn't have the time" -- its way harder to write a two-page memo/pitch than a fifty page one.

(4/5)

the best path is to just leave the first page totally blank.

writing is 100% a volume game, there's some golden ratio, I'm not sure what it is.

Hemingway has a quote: "I write one page of masterpiece to ninety-one pages of shit, and I try to put the shit in the wastebasket."

so that tells you, at the highest level of the game, you need 91 pages of volume to yield 1 good page

from personal experience (not that mine is worth a shit relative to his), something like 3:1 or 4:1 is realistic

to write a 250-page book, you need to produce 1000 pages of volume. thats the relatively easy part (with practice). the hard and shitty part is editing - from those 1000 pages, "killing ur darlings," cutting out the 750 pages of crap to get to 250 pages of quality

(5/5)

only after the 1000 pages of volume have been produced, should you even consider the first page.

you sit down and ask: "what exactly did I write here?"

the first page/intro will come from that, and it will help determine the path from 1000 --> 250.

along that path you'll probably rewrite the first page a bunch more times and torture urself, and it might even be better to wait until you get to 250

but the point is the same - the first page/intro is the OUTPUT of the writing and not the INPUT that determines all the rest.

--

last, on LLMs...matter of opinion, but my view is that any/all LLM-generated writing, even a summary, sticks out like a sore thumb...cant describe why, it just does.

better to write something 7/10 quality in ur own voice, with flaws and logical gaps, than 10/10 in LLM voice. readers are laser sharp on this shit, theyre looking to nail ppl, and this will dynamic will only continue as sloppification goes exponential.

good luck, and "BE YOURSELF - EVERYONE ELSE IS TAKEN."
